The researchers selected a virtual subsonic aircraft and designed a circular convergent nozzle to meet the mission requirements.
Various nozzle configurations were designed by changing the geometric profiles, including different exit aspect ratios (AR) and curvatures.
The researchers used a compressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier CFD code to analyze the thermal flow field and nozzle surface temperature distribution.
The IR signatures of the plume and nozzle surface were calculated using a narrow-band model and the RadThermIR code.
As the nozzle exit aspect ratio and curvature increased, the plume and nozzle surface temperatures decreased, leading to a reduction in the overall IR signature.
The non-circular nozzle configurations showed a decrease in thrust of up to 10.7% compared to the circular nozzle.
The plume IR signature showed peaks in the 4-4.5 μm and 6-7 μm wavelength bands, corresponding to the absorption bands of CO2 and H2O.
The researchers validated the accuracy of their CFD simulations by comparing the results to experimental data from the 1st AIAA Propulsion Aerodynamics Workshop.
The researchers found that the IR signature reduction must be balanced with other performance considerations, such as thrust, when designing the nozzle configuration.
The study provides qualitative information on the effects of nozzle configuration on the IR signature of a UAV, which can be useful for IR signature reduction design.
The researchers designed 20 different nozzle configurations by varying the exit aspect ratio (AR 2, AR 6, AR 8) and curvature (4 levels).
The maximum reduction in plume and nozzle surface IR signature was observed for the nozzle with the highest exit aspect ratio (AR 10) and largest curvature.
The researchers found that the nozzle exit aspect ratio and curvature had a greater impact on reducing the IR signature compared to the circular nozzle.
The study demonstrates the importance of considering both IR signature and other performance metrics, such as thrust, when designing aircraft propulsion systems.
The narrow-band model used in the study divided the 100-1000 cm-1 wavelength range into smaller bands to calculate the average spectral properties.
